newsitem.title: USA: Deciphering laundry lingo, rental car tips.
newsitem.headline: Deciphering laundry lingo, rental car tips.

text.p: There are scads of laundry detergents for sale in the average supermarket, but selecting the right cleaning product has become complicated business. The problem is deciphering the laundry lingo.
Good Housekeeping, in the July issue, has translated what the packages say and what they really mean.

When the package says "ultra," it means that it is a concentrated formula and half the amount of ordinary detergents do the job. The packages are easier to carry, but consumers used to eyeballing the amount of detergent may accidentally add too much.

When the package says "fabric softener added," it means just that. This kind of laundry product is cheaper than buying two different products but it doesn't generally clean as well as ordinary detergents and doesn't soften as well as regular fabric softener.

When the package says "more stain fighters," it means it has enzymes to remove tough stains, but make sure they are listed on the product. These products dissolve tough stains better than most detergents but don't eliminate the need to pretreat heavy stains.

When the package says "with bleach," it means a mild colour-safe bleach is added. These laundry products work better than ordinary detergents at whitening, brightening and removing stains. However this type of laundry product doesn't work as well as bleach that's added separately and should not be used on clothes with "no bleach" warning labels.

When the package says "free from dyes and perfumes," it means that scent and colouring typically added to detergents are absent. It is important for people with sensitive skin but if you want the "scent of clenliness," the magazine notes, these detergents are not for you.

When the package says "keeps clothes looking new" or "color protection," it means it deposits brighteners onto clothing, contains enzymes that sever pills and fuzz from cotton fabrics and prevents fading by neutralising trace levels of chlorine from the water. If this is the only type of detergent you use, clothes will look newer longer. But if clothes are already faded or gray, the damage can not be reversed, Good Housekeeping says.
Plan on renting a car this summer? Better make your reservations early and don't expect any bargains.
Blame it on skyrocketing demand for speciality vehicles and an overall tightening of the automobile rental market as companies streamline their fleets, according to SmartMoney magazine's July issue.

Alternatives to higher priced name-brand rental companies may be found just around your corner. The magazine advises that if you don't need the security blanket of a rental car brand that advertises nationally, "you may be able to find what you want -- and at a better prices -- at smaller or even local auto-rental outfits that specialise in particular vehicle types, from sport-utility to sports cars."
However, local companies often offer less flexibility when it comes to options such as pick-up in one city and drop-off in another.

Another tip, courtesy of Tom Parsons, editor of Best Fares. Check that magazine's web site for daily updates on rental deals, "which frequently come and go in the blink of an eye" (http://www.bestfares.com).
Zillions, the Consumer Reports magazine for kids, has named the ultimate way to beat the summer heat -- Super Soaker, the Rambo-style water shooter.

Out of eight items evaluated for their warm weather fun potential in the July/August issue, Super Soaker CPS 2000 ($30 Larami), topped the list. Among the 19 kids who tested the toys for Zillions, "most drenched testers agreed the Super Soaker was a great way to beat the heat, despite its fully loaded weight of 10 lbs."

Among other toys for summer fun, the Trapp Ball ($17 Saturnian I Inc.) was highly rated. Grip the net's handles, bring them together to cradle the rubber ball, then pull them apart to launch. For added fun, the testers recommended substituting a soaked spongy ball or a water balloon for the rubber ball.

Rated good was the Aerobie Jelly Disc ($4 Superflight Inc.) It quivers and jiggles as it flies through the air. One tester who liked the flexible design said "it feels like a bowl of Jell-O." Others found that they couldn't toss the disc very far.

Splash See-Thru Squirter (59 cents JA-RU) also got a good rating. This is a simple, old-fashioned squirt gun but because of its small size, it need refilling constantly. Testers liked its small size and suitability for sneak attacks.
Nerf Hydro Ball ($5 Kenner) was also rated good. Soak the Hydro Ball and you've got a water bomb that sprays, but doesn't explode, on impact. "You can hit people and it won't hurt," one tester said.

Rating only fair was the Big Bubba Bubble Maker ($10 Cap Toys). The testers found that while the battery-driven bubble maker made huge bubbles, the motorized fans in two bubble makers broke after less than a half hour of use.

Max Flight Frisbee ($9 Wham-O) also got a fair rating. None of Zillion's testers could make it fly more than 15 feet. While Wham-O said its special design allows it to fly up to 350 feet, one tester said, "I don't think it flew any different from other Frisbees."

Velcro Tag ($20 Velcro) also got a fair rating. Wearing Velcro vests, two players throw Velcro-covered balls at each other. Several testers said getting hit in the chest was a painful experience and one said, "My hair got caught in the vest and it hurt."
